questions.answer: Academic opportunities

questions.question: Please explain: *
Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: UiO, unlike UCPH, offers maritime law courses and a maritime law LLM and I want to work with maritime law

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer:
It was quite easy. The website is not ideal, but a lot of information can be found with some patience. Information on course registration was not straight forward, but if you read the e-mails etc. and have patience and faith, you'll get there. 
Additionally, the semester starts off with a buddy/intro week, where you can ask questions. 

I had to “argue” with the helpdesk to get the correct dates on my Erasmus, so be aware of that.

Also be aware of the fact that the contact person at the law faculty is practically impossible to reach. You have to CC the faculty itself on your e-mails, when you try to get in touch with her.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: None really

questions.question: What options were available for on campus housing? *
What options were available for meal plans or cooking facilities? *
What should future exchange students know about living in on campus housing? *
How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer:
The signing up on the waiting list itself is pretty easy. The problem is the distribution of housing. I applied for student housing closer to the city centre, since it was implied that everyone would find housing through SIO and that you would just be given another student house, if the ones you applied for were full. I applied in December, and still I was one of the very last to receive a housing offer. Some people never got an offer. The process was awful. I didn’t know if I had a place to stay just weeks before moving to Oslo. I got my offer in July. And no one could tell me anything about the process or let me know whether I should expect to get housing or not. Horrible experience. They had promised that the distribution was done by 20 June, but they could not keep that promise. 

Luckily, I did get a room in a student house in Sogn, where I shared kitchen and bath with six other students. It was honestly much better than I feared: the building was renovated, it’s close to the station, close to nature, but still not too far away from the city centre – and it’s nice to have some friends at home, even though it means sharing everything. 

I recommend applying for housing in Sogn and Kringsjå as your first priorities, as this increases your chances of finding a cheap place to live in Oslo – I think, again the process is a mystery.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer:
Oslo is surrounded by nature. Appreciate that you can live thirty minutes away from the city centre and be able to hike in your backyard. 

The student villages are actually quite nice.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer:
You receive an e-mail about what courses you can apply to. Remember that you can actually apply to more courses than they tell you – just look at the full course list on the website, for instance you can take classes in Norwegian as a Dane. When you apply for these courses, you just have to send an e-mail to the law faculty, and they will sign you up for that course. 

For the rest of the courses, you have to use the login that you receive via sms some time before registration opens and use it to login to Studentweb. Then you just apply for the courses that you want. You should definitely apply for more courses than you need – I applied for 50 ECTS and got them all – later you can withdraw from the courses. 

I recommend applying as quickly as possible. I heard rumours that the courses a allocated on a “first come first served” basis, but I honestly don’t know if it’s true. Anyways, I applied pretty much the day registration opened and I got all my courses immediately. The Norwegian students don’t apply until after the first week or two have passed. 

There were quite some frustrations with the registration the first couple of weeks in my kitchen and in general, but I think that the problems sort of fixed themselves over time. I know that not everyone got the courses they were hoping for, but just keep in touch with your faculty and you’ll find a solution.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: Every faculty has its own helpdesk that you can contact over the phone, via e-mail or just in person. It is quite easy to find a contact person on the website.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I got all the courses I wanted without any problems.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Apply for more ECTS than you need and do it when registration opens. No reason to wait.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer:
They don’t use reading lists. They tell you what the curriculum is, and each lecture has a name/heading, but they expect you to guess what part of the curriculum is relevant for each lecture. I prefer the structure of UCPH. 

I had no seminars, only lectures. It was fine. The classes were rather small. 

No groupwork. Nothing to hand in. We didn’t practice the exam, so the first time we really saw an exam paper was at the exam. I know that some of the other courses were more structured, especially those in Norwegian, but it was a general experience that UiO lacked structure compared to the Danish way.  

I just want to emphasize that I really liked my courses, despite preferring the UCPH structure. Many of the lecturers were specialists within their fields and it’s a huge bonus.

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your second semester. *
What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
Maritime Law: Safety, Competition and EU 

Even if you haven’t thought about maritime law yet, it’s a very interesting course. It mainly focuses on current issues within shipping and it’s a chance for you to explore some new topics without reading 1.000 pages on the legal aspects of shipping. Highly recommended. A great opportunity to become a shipping nerd.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: My Danish phone provider only allowed me to use data outside of Denmark for four months. It was not unexpected as I knew it before I left, but I guess it could be unexpected for some. I just got an eSim in Norway to cover my data use in addition to my Danish subscription.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer:
The Norwegian prices are very much like the Danish. Yes, groceries are a bit more expensive, but if you live in Copenhagen, you won’t be surprised by the prices in Oslo. Note that beer/alcohol is quite expensive and that the rules about alcohol are different from Denmark. 
 
Public transport for a month as a student is however cheap. 466 NOK to travel with all public transport in the city.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: SIO is a great option for students in Oslo. They offer both housing and cheap gyms all around town in addition to hosting social activities. I recommend becoming a member of SIO Sports. They have six gyms that offer a wide range of activities, e.g. yoga, swimming, bouldering etc.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Many of the clubs/associations offers free introduction lessons/hikes etc. Just go have fun and try a lot of stuff. I went on a hike with OSI Friluft and that was great

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer:
I went to Tromsø and Trondheim during my exchange. I didn't go to Lofoten simply because I had no time left. 
I flew to Tromsø with some friends from my kitchen and I took the train (Dovrebanen) to Trondheim alone. Both trips were great, but I especially liked the train ride to Trondheim, very beautiful and a nice little getaway. 

Oslo also has a lot to offer, e.g. the islands in the fiord, Ekebergparken, the forest etc.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Very easy. The Norwegians are basically Danes with ski.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Take Norwegian courses or join a club

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: The lack of rye bread and decent cheese. I ended up having rye bread delivered by my parents to Oslo like the other Danes.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: Being outdoor is a big part of the Norwegian culture and it's great

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1.	Have patience. Everything will be alright despite your initial frustrations over UiO. 
2.	Travel. Exchange is fun and as a student you can get some pretty great prices on trains/flights in Norway, so go explore! 
3.	Enjoy your stay. Grades are not everything, so spend some time on your hobbies and go on some hikes with new friends.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Norway is a lot like Denmark, so don't worry too much. Remember Copenhagen is only 1 hour away by flight, so you can always go home for a weekend if you feel like it.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Making a second home with good friends abroad

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Understanding how UiO works

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
